stats.label: Customer requests on the new platform

chapters.title: The old crossing
chapters.caption: The order system Fernhill built in {{project.monolith_year}}. It still carries every request Keystone has not moved yet, which is why it cannot come down early.

blocks.text:
Fernhill's order management system went live in {{project.monolith_year}}. By early 2025 it held {{project.monolith_loc|compact}} lines of Java in a single repository and shipped {{delivery.deploys_then}}, each release a weekend of work. A change took a median {{delivery.lead_then}} to reach customers, and {{delivery.cfr_then}} of releases needed a fix or a rollback.

The cost showed up at the checkout. Its slowest requests took {{experience.p95_then}}, and every peak season began with a code freeze because nobody trusted a release in November.

Keystone's plan was the **strangler pattern**: build new services beside the old system, move traffic one capability at a time, and keep the monolith running as the fallback until the last capability has crossed. The paintings on this page take that literally. The old trestle stays up until the new stone span can carry everything it carries.

chapters.title: Laying the piers
chapters.caption: The first phase moved no traffic at all. It built the parts every later service stands on.

blocks.text:
Nothing a customer could see shipped in the first phase. The team built a paved road instead: one pipeline template, shared clusters, an event bus and tracing that follows an order across services. Every service since has started from that template on its first day.

The payoff is in the four delivery measures the industry tracks. Deploys went from {{delivery.deploys_then}} to {{delivery.deploys_now}}, about {{delivery.deploy_ratio}} as many. Lead time fell from {{delivery.lead_then}} to {{delivery.lead_now}}.

steps.text: **July 2025.** The catalog read API goes first, in shadow mode, answering requests the monolith also answers so the two can be compared. Product pages are the bulk of all traffic, so the share jumps once reads switch over.
**October 2025.** Carts cross. For the first time the new platform holds customer state, not just reads.
**November to February.** The share stands still. Black Friday exposed a retry storm between the two systems, and the team spent three months on reliability before moving anything else.
**March 2026.** Checkout crosses, the hardest move so far, and the share passes half.
**Since June.** Payments run on both platforms, {{migration.payments_dual_run}} of authorisations on the new one. The cutover on {{migration.payments_cutover|date}} finishes the fourth arch.

chapters.title: The flood
chapters.caption: Black Friday 2025, a little before ten in the morning.

blocks.text:
Seven weeks after carts crossed, the busiest morning of the year found the gap between the two systems. A slow response from the monolith's inventory sync triggered retries, the retries multiplied, and the flood of events backed up into the cart service until its database had no connections left.

Checkout errors peaked at {{reliability.incident_peak_err}}. Customers felt it for {{reliability.incident_minutes}}, and analytics estimates {{reliability.incident_carts}} carts were abandoned in that window.

blocks.title: Forty-seven minutes, step by step
blocks.subtitle: Cart API error rate, Eastern time. Step through the response.

steps.title: The retries start
steps.text: The monolith's inventory sync times out and retries without backoff. Event volume on the cart topic rises eightfold.

steps.title: The queue backs up
steps.text: Consumer lag on cart events passes {{reliability.incident_lag|compact}} messages.

steps.title: The pool runs dry
steps.text: All {{reliability.incident_pool}} database connections in the cart service are in use. Requests queue, then fail.

steps.title: The page fires
steps.text: The SLO burn-rate alert pages the on-call engineer, who acknowledges within a minute and opens an incident.

steps.title: Walk the traffic back
steps.text: The incident commander routes cart traffic back to the monolith, which the strangler design kept warm for exactly this. Errors start to fall.

steps.title: Stop the flood
steps.text: The inventory sync is paused at the source and the lag drains.

steps.title: Recovered
steps.text: Errors are back under one percent. The postmortem produced {{reliability.incident_actions}} actions; all were closed by the end of January.

blocks.text: We didn't fix the new bridge that morning. We walked the traffic back across the old one, and then we fixed it.
blocks.role: incident commander, Cart and Checkout lead

blocks.text: Keep the old path warm until the new one has survived a peak. The fallback route turned what could have been a day-long outage into {{reliability.incident_minutes}}, and this year's load test ran at {{reliability.loadtest_multiple}} last year's peak.

blocks.title: What could still go wrong
blocks.subtitle: Open risks by likelihood and impact. Select one for the mitigation.

items.title: Payments cutover lands just before peak season
items.text: The cutover is set for {{migration.payments_cutover|date}}, thirteen days before the code freeze. Mitigation: the dual-run stays live through December so payments can fall back in minutes.

items.title: Monolith licence renews if decommission slips
items.text: Missing the June 2027 exit triggers a {{migration.license_renewal}} renewal. Mitigation: negotiate a three-month extension option now.

items.title: Scope keeps growing
items.text: Scope has grown {{plan.scope_growth_pct}} since kickoff, about {{plan.growth_recent}} a sprint lately. Mitigation: freeze fulfillment scope at the current epics.

items.title: Two people hold the ledger knowledge
items.text: Reconciliation logic lives in two engineers' heads. Mitigation: pairing rotation and written runbooks, half done.

items.title: Third-party logistics API limits
items.text: The 3PL partner caps requests per minute below our projected peak. Mitigation: batching and a queue in the adapter.

items.title: Peak-season capacity
items.text: Load tested at {{reliability.loadtest_multiple}} last year's peak in September. Watch item only.

blocks.text: The clearest result is at the checkout. Its slowest requests took {{experience.p95_then}} when the project began and take {{experience.p95_now}} now; most of that drop came the week checkout moved in March. Conversion followed: {{experience.conversion_then}} before, {{experience.conversion_now}} now, a gain of {{experience.conversion_gain}}.

blocks.text: The bill has not followed yet. For as long as both systems run, Fernhill pays for both: {{cost.dual_run}} a month in cloud spend on top of the data centre. The saving arrives only when the monolith is switched off, so every month of delay has a price.

{{project.engineers}} work on Keystone in {{project.squads}} squads, each owning its services from design to pager. In the last year {{project.contributors}} people merged code across {{project.repos}} repositories, {{delivery.prs_merged}} pull requests since kickoff. The median wait for a first review fell from {{delivery.review_hours_then}} to {{delivery.review_hours_now}}.

blocks.title: When does the last arch land?
blocks.subtitle: Drag the pace and the scope growth. The projection updates the finish date.
blocks.text: A straight-line projection from the last six sprints; it ignores holidays and the peak freeze, so treat the date as the earliest likely.

**Three decisions for this review.** First, confirm the payments cutover on {{migration.payments_cutover|date}} with the fallback kept warm through December. Second, freeze fulfillment scope at its current epics; at the recent pace the last arch lands on {{plan.forecast_finish|date}}, {{plan.forecast_weeks_late}} after the March target. Third, approve the licence extension option, so a slip past June costs a quarter of a renewal instead of a full year.
